items.stimulus:
In most drug trials, a comparison group receives a placebo: a pill that looks identical to the medicine but contains no active ingredient. Surgery is harder to test in this way. A patient knows whether they have had an operation, and the experience of being operated on can itself make people feel better. To separate the effect of the procedure from the effect of the experience, some researchers use sham surgery. Patients in the comparison group are given an anaesthetic and a small incision, but the key step of the operation is not carried out.

Critics argue that this crosses a line. A sugar pill is harmless, but an incision is not: it carries risks of infection, bleeding and reactions to anaesthesia, and the patient who receives the sham can gain nothing medically from it. Doctors, they say, have a duty not to harm the person in front of them, and that duty should not be set aside for the sake of future patients.

This objection deserves to be taken seriously, but it is not decisive. When sham-controlled trials have been carried out, a number of operations that surgeons were confident about have performed no better than the sham. Before those trials, many patients each year were exposed to the full risks of procedures that, it turned out, offered them little. Refusing to run a sham-controlled trial does not avoid harm; it shifts the harm from a small number of volunteers to a much larger number of future patients.

Nor is deception necessarily involved. Participants can be told in advance that they have an equal chance of receiving either the real or the sham procedure, and they are free to decline to take part.

None of this means that sham surgery is always acceptable. It is justified only when there is genuine doubt about whether the real operation works, when the risks of the sham are kept as low as possible, and when participants fully understand what they are agreeing to. Where these conditions are met, the greater wrong may lie in continuing to operate without knowing.

items.stimulus:
In most drug trials, a comparison group receives a placebo: a pill that looks identical to the medicine but contains no active ingredient. Surgery is harder to test in this way. A patient knows whether they have had an operation, and the experience of being operated on can itself make people feel better. To separate the effect of the procedure from the effect of the experience, some researchers use sham surgery. Patients in the comparison group are given an anaesthetic and a small incision, but the key step of the operation is not carried out.

Critics argue that this crosses a line. A sugar pill is harmless, but an incision is not: it carries risks of infection, bleeding and reactions to anaesthesia, and the patient who receives the sham can gain nothing medically from it. Doctors, they say, have a duty not to harm the person in front of them, and that duty should not be set aside for the sake of future patients.

This objection deserves to be taken seriously, but it is not decisive. When sham-controlled trials have been carried out, a number of operations that surgeons were confident about have performed no better than the sham. Before those trials, many patients each year were exposed to the full risks of procedures that, it turned out, offered them little. Refusing to run a sham-controlled trial does not avoid harm; it shifts the harm from a small number of volunteers to a much larger number of future patients.

Nor is deception necessarily involved. Participants can be told in advance that they have an equal chance of receiving either the real or the sham procedure, and they are free to decline to take part.

None of this means that sham surgery is always acceptable. It is justified only when there is genuine doubt about whether the real operation works, when the risks of the sham are kept as low as possible, and when participants fully understand what they are agreeing to. Where these conditions are met, the greater wrong may lie in continuing to operate without knowing.

Over the past two decades, many schools have quietly reduced the time spent teaching handwriting. Keyboards, it is said, are the tools of the modern world, and hours spent practising joined-up letters would be better spent elsewhere. This is a mistake, and the time has come to reverse it.

The first reason is that handwriting is not simply a slower way of producing text. When children form letters by hand, they must attend to the shape of each one, and this attention appears to help them recognise letters when they read. In a study of 120 six-year-olds in the town of Ellmere, children who practised writing new letters by hand recognised them more accurately a week later than children who practised typing them.

The second reason concerns note-taking. Because most people write more slowly than they type, students taking notes by hand cannot record a lecture word for word. They are forced to choose what matters and put it in their own words, and it is this selection, not the recording, that helps them remember.

Some will object that adults now rarely write anything by hand, so the skill is obsolete. But the same could be said of mental arithmetic, which few people need now that calculators are everywhere; we still teach it because it builds understanding. Others argue that the timetable is already full. Yet handwriting need not take much time: fifteen minutes a day in the early years would be enough.

Finally, handwriting is a matter of independence. A child who can write needs no device, no charger and no network connection to record a thought. Any school that has abandoned handwriting lessons has therefore left its pupils helpless whenever technology fails.

Restoring handwriting will not solve every problem in education. But it is cheap, it is supported by evidence, and it gives children something no machine can take away.

items.stimulus:
When speakers of one language adopt a word from another, the borrowed word rarely arrives unchanged. Borrowing usually begins with bilingual speakers, who use a foreign word because it names something new, such as a tool, a food or a legal idea, for which their own language has no ready term. If the word proves useful, speakers who know only one language pick it up from them, and at this stage it starts to be reshaped.

The first changes are usually to sound. A word is fitted to the patterns of the borrowing language: groups of consonants that are not allowed may be broken up by added vowels, and unfamiliar sounds are replaced by the nearest native ones. Speakers of Pelor, a fictional island language in which no word may end in a consonant, turned the trading word 'kast' into 'kasta'.

Meaning changes too, often more slowly. A borrowed word frequently takes on a narrower meaning than it had in the source language, because it entered with one particular use. In Pelor, 'marenu', from a mainland word meaning any kind of boat, came to mean only the large cargo vessels that first brought the word to the island.

Eventually a loanword may become so thoroughly absorbed that speakers no longer recognise it as foreign. It takes native grammatical endings, combines with native words and is even used to build new words of its own. At this point it is foreign only in its history.

The process can also run in reverse. Sometimes a loanword, transformed in its new home, is borrowed back into its language of origin with its altered sound and meaning, and is then treated there as a foreign word.

items.stimulus:
In many towns of medieval Europe, a person could not simply set up as a weaver, baker or goldsmith. The right to practise a craft was controlled by a guild, an association of the town's masters in that trade, and guilds placed considerable obstacles in the way of newcomers. A typical path began with an apprenticeship lasting several years, followed by a period as a paid journeyman. Only then might a candidate apply to become a master, often by producing a 'masterpiece' for inspection and paying a substantial entry fee. In many guilds, these fees were reduced or waived for the sons of existing masters.

Historians disagree about why these barriers existed. One view emphasises quality. Buyers in a medieval market had few ways of judging goods before purchase: cloth might be stretched to look longer, or precious metal mixed with cheaper ones. By examining every new master's skill and punishing poor workmanship, a guild offered customers a guarantee, and protected the reputation of the town's products in distant markets.

A second view emphasises income. By limiting the number of masters, guilds reduced competition and allowed existing members to charge higher prices. On this account, long apprenticeships provided masters with cheap labour, and the favourable treatment of masters' sons shows that the aim was to keep the trade's profits within a small circle of families.

The two explanations are not mutually exclusive. A rule that kept out unskilled workers would also, inevitably, keep out some competitors, and masters had every reason to present self-interested restrictions in the language of quality. What evidence might separate them? If restrictions were mainly about quality, one would expect them to be strictest in trades where faults were hard for buyers to detect. If they were mainly about income, one would expect them to tighten when demand fell and members' earnings were threatened.

items.stimulus:
An ancient puzzle asks us to imagine a famous wooden ship preserved in a harbour. As its planks rot, each is replaced with a new one, until eventually none of the original timber remains. Is it still the same ship?

Many people answer yes. At every stage most of the ship's parts were ones it had had the day before, and it kept its shape, its name and its function. On this view, what makes something the same object over time is continuity: gradual change, with no sudden break, preserves identity.

A later version of the puzzle makes this answer harder to hold. Suppose a collector has kept every discarded plank and, once the last one is removed, reassembles them all in their original arrangement. Now there are two ships. The repaired ship has the better claim to continuity; the reassembled ship has every one of the original parts. If both claims are good, it seems we must say that one ship has become two. But a single thing cannot be identical to two different things.

Some philosophers conclude that the question 'Is it the same ship?' has no hidden fact behind it waiting to be discovered. We have a practice of naming and tracking objects, and in ordinary cases continuity of parts and continuity of form go together, so the practice works smoothly. The puzzle simply separates two features that normally come as a pair, and our concept was never designed to say which matters more. On this view, the sensible response is not to search harder for the answer but to decide, for a given purpose, which feature we care about. A museum interested in authentic materials might favour the reassembled ship; a harbour authority registering vessels might favour the repaired one.

What began as a scheduling convenience for private companies thus reshaped how whole societies experience the day. The time on our clocks is not the time of the Sun overhead, but an agreement, one made originally for the sake of trains.

items.question: A row of joined squares is made from matchsticks. One square uses 4 matchsticks, two joined squares use 7, and three joined squares use 10, with each new square added to the end of the row. A row made in this way uses exactly 100 matchsticks. How many squares does it contain?
